thread.title: Here's how Triad stocks fared this week

author: Jeff Jeffrey
title: Here's how Triad stocks fared this week
text: – Triad   2:29pm EST Stock markets took a wild ride Tuesday following a record-setting selloff Feb. 5 that sent shockwaves throughout the U.S. economy. But even after rebounding from a 500-point loss Wednesday, major stock indices continued to waver from positive to negative territory throughout much of the day. As the markets neared the afternoon closing, the wave of volatility had pushed the Dow Jones Industrial Average back to nearly 24,700 — a nearly 1,000-point swing. Wall Street experts said the broader declines, which began in earnest Jan. 29, might be driven by investor worries that the economy is entering a period of steeper than normal inflation. The recent losses have been widespread and industry agnostic. Among the biggest losers as of Monday was Seattle-based radio technology and software maker Impinj Inc. (Nasdaq: PI), which saw its stock price plummet 45 percent to $11.94 between Jan. 29 and Feb. 5. Other companies that took double-digit hits to their stock prices included Overstock.com (Nasdaq: OSTK), down 36 percent to $49.50; Eastman Kodak Co. (NYSE: KODK) down 35 percent to $6.20; and Bellicum Pharmaceuticals (Nasdaq: BLCM) down 35 percent to $5.61. In the Triad, vTv Therapeutics (NASDAQ: VTVT) took the biggest hit in stock price, as shares decreased by 12 percent since Jan. 29. But share prices have actually increased since Jan. 2, up 12 percent as of Feb. 7. As of noon Thursday, vTv Therapeutics shares were trading at $6.92, according to Yahoo Finance. Tanger Factory (NYSE: SKT) shares decreased by almost 8 percent from $25.40 on Jan. 29 to $23.54 on Feb. 7. As of noon Thursday, shares were trading at $23.52. Qorvo (NASDAQ: QRVO) shares actually increased by 15 percent since Jan. 29, and by 13 percent since Jan. 2. Some Triad companies saw little change in stock price. Unifi Inc. (NYSE: UFI) shares remained fairly constant at about $36. Primo Water Corp.'s shares decreased by about 5 percent from Jan. 29 to Feb. 7, though had little overall change from Jan. 2 to Feb. 7. Old Dominion Freight Line , Culp Inc., Hanesbrands Inc., BB&T Corp. and VF Corp. all saw at or below a 4 percent decrease in stock price. Here's a breakdown of the public Triad companies with the most change (positive or negative) from Jan. 29 to Feb. 7. The slide follows a stretch that saw U.S. stocks hit historic highs amid investor excitement over strong corporate earnings reports, a growing economy and the passage of a business-friendly tax bill. Last month, the stalwart Dow Jones Industrial Average took just seven days to add 1,000 points and surpass 26,000 for the first time in its history. The Nasdaq and S&P 500 also set new records in the early days of 2018. Markets took a sharp turn last week, and the declines accelerated through Monday, with the Dow tumbling to a low of 24,085 as of today's opening bell. Gina Martin Adams , chief equity strategist for Bloomberg Intelligence , said investors were overly optimistic in 2017 amid a steady stream of strong corporate earnings reports. But a number of sectors have been rocked by developments that created something of a contagion effect heading into this week's selloff, Adams said. For example, health care stocks spiraled in the wake of the joint announcement by Amazon (Nasdaq: AMZN), Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRK.A) and JPMorgan Chase (NYSEL: JPM) of plans to create a joint health care venture aimed at reducing health care costs for employees. Similar reverberations hit the tech sector with Apple’s (Nasdaq: AAPL) introduction of an update to its health app that will enable customers to view medical records on their phones. Add in disappointing earnings reports from ExxonMobil (NYSE: XOM) and Chevron (NYSE: CVX), and some investors are feeling the heat, spurring fears that ultimately rippled through the broader market, Adams said. “There were some pretty big losses in some specialized products,” Adams said. “It seems to be a symptom of a deflation of the excess of investor optimism." “It’s still a bull market,” Adams said. “As long as the fundamentals of the market are strong, which they are, I don’t see that changing.”
